analysis.one_liner: Bans three classes of toxic pesticides, suspends pesticides banned abroad, and adds farmworker safety protections.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it sat in the House Agriculture Committee from July 2023 until Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have overhauled the nation's pesticide law. It would have immediately canceled all uses of organophosphate pesticides, neonicotinoid pesticides, and paraquat; automatically suspended any pesticide already banned by the European Union or Canada; ended the sale of leftover stocks of banned pesticides; required labels to list hidden 'inert' ingredients; and created new protections for farmworkers, including mandatory reporting of pesticide injuries, fines for employers who fail to report, and penalties for retaliating against workers who report. It also would have let local communities adopt pesticide restrictions stricter than state rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmworkers, who face the heaviest pesticide exposure, would gain mandatory injury reporting with fines and criminal penalties for employers who hide incidents or retaliate, bilingual labels, and anonymous reporting channels. Children and rural residents would gain from the outright bans on chemicals linked to neurodevelopmental harm and Parkinson's disease. Communities that want local pesticide restrictions, pollinators and the farms that depend on them, and citizens who want to sue EPA for non-enforcement would all gain.

how_it_helps.text: Farmworkers would get mandatory employer reporting of pesticide injuries and deaths, with fines starting at $1,000 per day for unreported incidents and criminal penalties up to $100,000 for covering them up or coercing workers not to report [S3].

Employers could not fire or punish workers for reporting pesticide harm or participating in enforcement proceedings, and immigration status could not be used against a worker based solely on a report [S3].

The bill would permanently cancel all uses of organophosphates, neonicotinoids, and paraquat, chemicals Congress's findings link to neurodevelopmental damage in children, pollinator collapse, and sharply increased Parkinson's risk [S2, S3].

Any pesticide banned by the European Union or Canada would be automatically suspended from use in the United States, addressing the roughly 72 pesticides the findings say are banned abroad but still used here [S2, S3].
Pesticide labels would have to list all inert ingredients, which the findings say can make up 99 percent of a product and include toxic chemicals [S2, S3].
Local governments could adopt pesticide protections stricter than their state's, reversing state preemption that has blocked community-level restrictions [S2, S3].
Any person could sue EPA in federal court for failing to carry out the pesticide law, and whistleblowers would get reinstatement and damages through Labor Department complaints [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers would bear the main cost, losing the market for three entire chemical classes and facing new reporting, labeling, and compliance requirements whose violation cancels their registrations. Conventional farmers and other users of these chemicals would lose tools they currently rely on, and enforcement duties would add costs for agribusiness employers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pesticide makers and conventional farm users

drawbacks.text: The three class-wide bans would take effect immediately by operation of law without case-by-case proceedings, removing crop-protection tools from growers of crops such as citrus, cotton, and vegetables who may lack ready substitutes, raising costs or reducing yields [S3].

Automatically suspending every pesticide banned by any EU member country or Canada would tie U.S. approvals to foreign regulatory decisions, and the bill prohibits EPA from weighing economic costs when reviewing those bans, a design its critics would call rigid [S3].

Automatic cancellation if EPA misses deadlines, and immediate suspension of any pesticide linked to a farmworker death pending review, trade administrative caution for speed, raising the risk that some products are pulled before EPA finishes its own scientific review [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health and labor protections are substantial and targeted at people with the least power: farmworkers and children. The real costs fall on pesticide manufacturers and on growers who would lose access to some tools, and the bill's automatic, class-wide bans would remove some flexibility from the regulatory process. An honest weighing favors the bill's protections for exposed workers and communities, while acknowledging that banning entire chemical classes without case-by-case review imposes real and unevenly distributed costs on agriculture.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced, sent to a subcommittee two months later, and never advanced further before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Jim McGovern and 13 original Democratic cosponsors introduced the bill on July 28, 2023 [S1, S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Agriculture the same day; the bill never received a hearing or a floor vote in that committee [S1, S5].
On September 26, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Conservation, Research, and Biotechnology, where it remained for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill ended the 118th Congress with 22 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no vote in either chamber [S4, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide manufacturers keep selling organophosphates, neonicotinoids, and paraquat, and growers keep using them; farmworkers and communities remain without the bill's protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pesticide manufacturers and their current customers

for.name: Jim McGovern
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 13 original Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 22 Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support; no Republican cosponsored the bill.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred and never advanced
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it was referred to a subcommittee on September 26, 2023 and died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the committee that buried it was chaired by Republicans, so no vote ever tested the bill's support.

industries.note: The bill would immediately and permanently cancel the entire organophosphate, neonicotinoid, and paraquat classes, ban products barred in the EU or Canada, force disclosure of inert ingredients, and require farmworker incident reporting, with automatic cancellation for noncompliance [S2, S3].

industries.industry: Conventional farming and agricultural chemical users
industries.note: Growers would lose access to some widely used crop-protection chemicals and face tighter emergency exemptions, while gaining from restored pollinator health and stronger protections for their hired workforce [S2, S3].

industries.industry: Organic growers and farms dependent on pollination
industries.note: Canceling neonicotinoids addresses the documented decline of bees and other pollinators, which supports crop yields and farms positioned around pesticide-free production [S2, S3].
